name: Uma Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers stay confidential, so you can tell me what you say outside and what you worry about privately. What is a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage four booking clerks for a large manufacturer's staff travel office. We book trains and hotels for engineers going to repair customer machines, then chase receipts and change tickets when a job runs late. I was made a junior manager in the spring. I know the travel rules, but I still miss exceptions in the monthly budget and the oldest clerk catches them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes you stay, and what is happening at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting an engineer home when the last train changes; a phone call has a person on the other end. I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and have never used an AI tool. My husband Owen repairs buses, and our daughter is fifteen and our son is eight. We have a mortgage, typical manager pay and about three months of expenses saved. There are some other travel offices nearby, but I don't want to uproot the children for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of automatic receipt filing would save us time, and people would still call when a train is cancelled. I could keep learning the manager's budget without another system landing on us. Three months saved isn't riches, but Owen's workshop hours have been steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the clerks to keep calling the hotel when a booking is wrong. I'd tell Owen the desk looks much the same and I can keep my wage. I wouldn't say a filing shortcut can handle an engineer stranded after midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is safe in this picture, but I worry about the ordinary mortgage and the daughter's school costs. The budget errors make me feel junior, even if my pay is normal. I would rather learn the old report properly before taking on another tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting Monday I'd have the senior clerk check the three unusual travel claims with me before the monthly report goes to finance. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep this role and put 120 a month into savings after the mortgage and school bills clear. If Owen loses workshop overtime, we'd pause that transfer before using credit to pretend we're saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about bills, though the job itself seems steady. A small change is still one more thing to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was unusual about a recent claim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An engineer's hotel receipt had two nights, but the work order showed one. The clerk noticed a train cancellation added the second night, so we paid it. I would have refused it if she'd not opened the work order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the filing tool if asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone showed me on a test receipt and finance approved it, I could look. I have never used an AI tool, and I am not volunteering to put real travel claims through one first. I need to know where the receipt goes.

say: I'd tell clerks to **call the hotel** when a booking is wrong.
I'd tell Owen my **travel wage stays** if AI only files some receipts.
think: My **job looks safe**, while mortgage and school costs still weigh on us.
I want to master the **old budget report** before adding another tool.
do: Check **three unusual claims** with the senior clerk before each monthly report.
Save **120 monthly** only after mortgage and school bills clear, pausing if Owen loses overtime.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about bills, though my role appears steady.
S0.quote: I need to know where the receipt goes.
fieldNote: A **second hotel night** shows why she checks work orders with the senior clerk.
Her job seems stable, but **mortgage and school costs** keep money on her mind.
She has **never used AI** and would look only at an approved test receipt.

steps.text: Check three unusual travel claims with the senior clerk before each monthly report
Save 120 monthly after mortgage and school bills unless Owen loses overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking, changing tickets, checking receipts and answering travellers are the whole team's day. A stronger system could do that before robots touch Owen's bus workshop. One clerk might handle complaints for four others, and as the newest manager I could be an easy salary to remove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our director that staff deserve a written timetable and actual training, not just a demo. I'd tell my clerks to keep accurate records of wrong bookings. I wouldn't pretend the desk will stay full when the work moves to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours or post could be cut, and Owen's wage would not cover everything at home. There are some other travel offices, but they'll have the same software offer. I don't use AI now, so I would be slower than the clerks who already know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask the director which bookings will be automated and request a written count of posts after the pilot. I'd keep taking the difficult hotel calls while the tool is tested and ask a clerk to show me one invented booking if the firm gives us paid learning time. I'd stop the weekend café meal and use that money to make the mortgage reserve last longer, while checking posted vacancies at the nearby offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own wage. Owen and I have worked hard for the house, and I don't want a demo to decide what it is worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a clerk teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, though I would rather learn quietly than fumble in front of the whole team. I know I am behind on this. If the firm expects us to learn, it should give us paid time and let us ask a foolish question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not leave for another travel office now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An advert isn't a signed job, and we have a mortgage. I'd apply if the pay and hours are clear, but I wouldn't quit first. The children need their school routines more than a brave story about starting over.

say: I'd ask the director for a **written staffing timetable** before rollout.
I'd tell clerks to record **wrong bookings** while the tool is tested.
think: My **own post could shrink**, and Owen's wage cannot cover all household bills.
I'm behind on AI and may be **slower than clerks** who know the tool.
do: Ask for a **post count** after the pilot and paid learning time.
Keep handling **difficult hotel calls** during the test.
Cut the **weekend café meal** and check nearby posted travel jobs.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my wage and the mortgage.
S1.quote: An advert isn't a signed job, and we have a mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **new manager standing** leaves her exposed when booking and checking move first.
She would try an **invented booking** on paid time, while protecting real traveller details.
She checks other offices but will **not resign** for an advert without clear terms.

steps.text: Learn one invented booking from a clerk if paid learning time is offered
Stop the weekend café meal while the travel pilot runs
Apply for nearby posted travel work only if pay and hours are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If full AGI can do almost all thinking work by 2028, it can book trips and solve the awkward hotel problem too. Owen may still repair buses with his hands until robots around 2031, but workshop ordering and paperwork change earlier. My travel desk could close well before the workshop does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the clerks the date on the card and ask for proper notice and paid openings. I'd tell Owen we need to count his wage against the mortgage and children's costs before a cut comes. In public I'd say families need work and apprenticeships, and any support should reach people who truly need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose my travel job by 2028, and Owen's wage alone is not enough for the mortgage, food and school costs. Three months of savings gives us a short window, not a new livelihood. My daughter would be seventeen then, and I don't want her plans decided by our lost wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now we'd stop paying toward the planned summer extension and keep that cash for bills. I'd ask the bus depot manager whether a paid parts-receiving opening exists, what it pays and whether supervised stock checks are part of it; I won't call its ordering desk safe from AGI. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk job ends, I'd apply only if the posted depot wage plus Owen's covers mortgage, food and school costs, and I'd ask my sister whether she can handle school pickup on training days before promising those hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can picture three mortgage statements arriving while I'm still looking for a place to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your daughter postpone her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't ask our daughter to choose a trade just because we're frightened, though I would show her the numbers. She might want an apprenticeship, and I'd help if she chose it. We will postpone the home extension, not choose our daughter's career for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you do in parts receiving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the delivered bus parts against labels and look for damaged boxes with a trained worker. The ordering and tracking might be automated in 2028, so I'd need paid physical duties. I couldn't walk into the workshop and claim to be a mechanic.

say: I'd ask for **notice and paid openings** before the travel desk closes.
I'd tell Owen we must count **his wage against bills** before making promises.
think: I expect my **travel wage to end** by 2028.
Three months saved and Owen's pay cannot cover **family bills** for long.
do: Pause the **summer extension fund** and keep the cash for bills now.
Ask for a **posted paid receiving role** with physical checks and a clear wage.
Ask my sister about **school pickup** before accepting training hours.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss and only three months of savings.
S2.quote: We will postpone the home extension, not choose our daughter's career for her.
fieldNote: She sees **2028 travel-desk loss** while Owen's physical repairs may last until 2031 robots.
Parts receiving needs **actual paid stock checks** and enough combined household income.
She protects her **daughter's choice** while postponing a planned home extension.

steps.text: Pause payments toward the summer home extension and keep cash for bills
Apply for posted bus-parts receiving work only if combined wages cover household essentials
Ask sister about school pickup before accepting any paid training hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to see if a paid parts-receiving shift exists before travel booking faces AGI in 2031. Its ordering and paperwork still change in 2031; hands-on box checks meet robots around 2034. A move would only buy time if the company actually keeps people for those physical checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our company to fund apprenticeships for workers it expects to move. I'd tell Owen we could try a paid shift before we give up my manager wage. I wouldn't call a course seat a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn parts receiving with enough supervised time, though I'm not quick with new systems. I would miss my office wage if the depot paid less. Five years could let us build more cash, but the mortgage and both children still need paying for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the bus depot for one paid shadow shift a month; if a place opens I'd complete the physical stock checks under a trained worker. I'd add 100 monthly to cash only while our wages cover mortgage, food and school costs. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted receiving role only if its wage plus Owen's covers those bills and my sister can cover any school pickups that overlap the shift; otherwise I'd keep searching paid work from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I have time to find out whether the shift suits me. That is more than the two-year picture offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might go wrong on a shadow shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might read a part number badly and send the wrong brake component to the mechanic. I'd ask someone experienced to check each label until I know the shelves. A bus repair is no place to prove I learn quickly by guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move house for a depot job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for an offer that covers a higher mortgage or travel cost, and not before talking to Owen and the children. Some similar offices are nearby, so I'd look there first. I don't want to make a home move based on a training flyer.

I'd tell Owen a **paid trial shift** comes before giving up my office wage.
think: I might learn **parts receiving** with enough supervised time, though I'm slow with systems.
A lower depot wage could still strain the **mortgage and children’s costs**.
do: Complete **monthly paid shadow shifts** if the depot offers a place.
Save **100 monthly** only while both wages cover household essentials.
Apply after 2031 for **posted receiving work** only if combined pay and school pickup fit.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test an actual paid shift.
S3.quote: A bus repair is no place to prove I learn quickly by guessing.
fieldNote: She asks for **supervised label checks** and admits she may struggle with part numbers.
The move needs **a paid vacancy** plus adequate wages and school pickup, all uncertain.
She separates **2031 ordering risk** from physical checks facing robots around 2034.

steps.text: Complete paid monthly parts-receiving shifts if the depot offers a place
Save 100 monthly only while both wages cover mortgage, food and school costs
Apply for receiving if combined wages cover mortgage, food, school costs and sister covers overlapping pickups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put me at 53, with our son eighteen and our daughter twenty-five. I would like the mortgage smaller by then, but I cannot count on it. Travel booking still faces AGI in 2036, and robots reach hands-on depot work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to pay for useful apprenticeships while the booking desk still has work. I'd tell other parents to keep their children's choices open rather than pick a trade for them. Family should help where it can, but a firm should train the workers whose work it changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to move into a paid stores job and build a stronger reserve before 2036. I don't imagine myself suddenly loving software; I would rather know the parts and the people who use them. The depot's planning still faces AGI and the box checks face later robots, so I would not call it lifetime safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask our training office whether it will fund a recognised parts-handling course with paid depot hours; if approved, I'd finish the course and supervised shifts while keeping my wage. I'd put 150 monthly into our emergency account after mortgage and school bills, pausing when Owen loses overtime. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted depot stores job only if its physical duties and combined pay cover our bills; if none exists, I'd stay through notice and search the other local employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than safe. Ten years is long enough to prepare if the company actually funds the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the training office says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the travel job and ask Owen to tell me when his depot posts a paid trainee place, without asking him to get me hired. I won't take a loan for a course that doesn't lead to work. Our mortgage is already a large enough promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want the children close to home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like it, but they will be adults by then. Our daughter should choose her own path, and our son will be old enough to decide his next step. I can offer them a room, not an order.

say: I'd ask for **employer-funded apprenticeship** while the booking desk still pays wages.
I'd tell parents to leave **children's choices** open, even when money is tight.
think: A paid stores job may give me **another wage**, but only if a place opens.
I would not treat depot work as **lifetime safety** after 2036 and 2039.
do: Complete a **funded parts course** with paid shifts only if approved.
Save **150 monthly** after bills, pausing when Owen loses overtime.
Take a **posted depot job** after 2036 only if physical duties and pay fit.
feel: I feel **uneasy** without a guaranteed funded route or later job.
S4.quote: Our mortgage is already a large enough promise.
fieldNote: She asks for **paid, recognised training**, with no personal loan if the company refuses.
Her savings transfer depends on **Owen's overtime** continuing after mortgage bills.
She lets her **grown children choose**, while recognising the depot bridge has a robot deadline.

steps.text: Complete funded parts-handling course and paid shifts only if the training office approves
Save 150 monthly after bills only while Owen’s overtime continues
Take posted physical depot stores work after 2036 only if combined pay covers household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Booking is thinking work and it could go before Owen's hands-on bus repairs change; his wage alone won't cover the mortgage and both children's costs. I'd need notice, a real paid opening and paid instruction in any new duties before leaving this desk. If my sister could cover the school pickup during training, that would help too, but I would ask first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who answers the engineer when the hotel says there is no room after the train has gone. I can ring the hotel back and hear a tired person trying to solve it. An automatic booking number isn't a bed for the night.

headlineQuote: An automatic booking number isn't a bed for the night.
portrait: Uma, **43**, became a junior manager of four travel clerks this spring at a large manufacturer.
She knows booking rules but still misses **budget exceptions**; she has never used AI tools and prefers direct calls.
She and Owen have **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with three months saved on typical manager and mechanic wages.
She would seek **paid, supervised work** if travel bookings vanish, while checking childcare and wages before any move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her travel office wage before she finds another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** and a real paid opening with instruction before she leaves the booking desk.
School pickup help from **her sister**, only if her sister can agree to it.
